claim: Studying the human subcortical auditory system non-invasively is challenging due to its small, densely packed structures deep within the brain.
source: Studying the human subcortical auditory system non-invasively is challenging due to its small, densely packed structures deep within the brain.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract describing the challenges of studying the subcortical auditory system.

claim: The elaborate three-dimensional (3-D) structure of the subcortical auditory system can be difficult to understand based on currently available 2-D schematics and animal models.
source: Additionally, the elaborate three-dimensional (3-D) structure of the system can be difficult to understand based on currently available 2-D schematics and animal models.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a challenge in understanding the system.

claim: The authors created anatomical atlases based on state-of-the-art human histology (BigBrain).
source: We created anatomical atlases based on state-of-the-art human histology (BigBrain) and postmortem MRI (50 µm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors created anatomical atlases based on postmortem MRI at 50 µm resolution.
source: We created anatomical atlases based on state-of-the-art human histology (BigBrain) and postmortem MRI (50 µm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors measured functional MRI (fMRI) responses to natural sounds.
source: We measured functional MRI (fMRI) responses to natural sounds and demonstrate that the functional localization of subcortical structures is reliable within individual participants who were scanned in two different experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used.

claim: The functional localization of subcortical structures is reliable within individual participants who were scanned in two different experiments.
source: We measured functional MRI (fMRI) responses to natural sounds and demonstrate that the functional localization of subcortical structures is reliable within individual participants who were scanned in two different experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: A group functional atlas derived from the functional data locates subcortical auditory structures with a median distance below 2 mm.
source: Further, a group functional atlas derived from the functional data locates these structures with a median distance below 2 mm.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: The authors revealed structural connectivity maps of the human subcortical auditory pathway both in vivo (1050 µm isotropic resolution) and post mortem (200 µm isotropic resolution) using diffusion MRI tractography.
source: Using diffusion MRI tractography, we revealed structural connectivity maps of the human subcortical auditory pathway both in vivo (1050 µm isotropic resolution) and post mortem (200 µm isotropic resolution).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods and results of the study.

claim: The organization of the auditory pathway is largely conserved across mammalian species.
source: This might be problematic because, while the organization of the auditory pathway is largely conserved across mammalian species (Malmierca and Hackett, 2010; Schofield, 2010), the form and function of each structure may not be analogous (Moore, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The form and function of each structure in the auditory pathway may not be analogous across mammalian species.
source: This might be problematic because, while the organization of the auditory pathway is largely conserved across mammalian species (Malmierca and Hackett, 2010; Schofield, 2010), the form and function of each structure may not be analogous (Moore, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Three human imaging modalities – histology, postmortem magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and in vivo MRI at ultra high-field (7 Tesla) – can identify the structures of the subcortical auditory pathway at high spatial resolution (between 50 and 1100 µm).
source: In this paper, we show that three human imaging modalities – histology, postmortem magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and in vivo MRI at ultra high-field (7 Tesla) – can identify the structures of the subcortical auditory pathway at high spatial resolution (between 50 and 1100 µm).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings of the study.

claim: Moore (1987) stained both myelin and the cell bodies of subcortical auditory structures in four postmortem human brainstem samples and compared them to the analogous structures in cats.
source: Moore (1987) stained both myelin and the cell bodies of subcortical auditory structures in four postmortem human brainstem samples and compared them to the analogous structures in cats (a common model for auditory investigations at the time).
evidence: This is a description of previous research cited in the paper.

claim: Moore et al. (1995) used myelin and Nissl cell body staining to investigate the timeline of myelination in human auditory brainstem development.
source: Later investigations from the same group Moore et al. (1995) used myelin and Nissl cell body staining to investigate the timeline of myelination in human auditory brainstem development.
evidence: This is a description of previous research cited in the paper.

claim: Kulesza (2007) stained six human brainstems for Nissl substance, focusing on the superior olivary complex, finding evidence of a substructure (the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body) whose existence in the human auditory system has been debated for decades.
source: More recently, Kulesza (2007) stained six human brainstems for Nissl substance, focusing on the superior olivary complex, finding evidence of a substructure (the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body) whose existence in the human auditory system has been debated for decades.
evidence: This is a description of previous research cited in the paper.

claim: Advances in post-mortem human MRI allow for investigating three-dimensional (3-D) brain anatomy with increasingly high resolution (100 µm and below).
source: Advances in post-mortem human MRI allow for investigating three-dimensional (3-D) brain anatomy with increasingly high resolution (100 µm and below).
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of current MRI technology.

claim: Postmortem MRI has provided useful information about laminar structure in the auditory cortex.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, postmortem MRI has not been utilized within the subcortical auditory system, although it has provided useful information about laminar structure in the auditory cortex (Wallace et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: To the best of the authors' knowledge, postmortem MRI has not been utilized within the subcortical auditory system prior to this study.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, postmortem MRI has not been utilized within the subcortical auditory system, although it has provided useful information about laminar structure in the auditory cortex (Wallace et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Anatomical in vivo MRI investigations of the human subcortical auditory pathway have focused on thalamic nuclei.
source: Anatomical in vivo MRI investigations of the human subcortical auditory pathway so far have focused on thalamic nuclei (Devlin et al., 2006; Moerel et al., 2015), and the identification of the acoustic radiations between the auditory cortex and medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus with diffusion-weighted MRI tractography (Devlin et al., 2006; Behrens et al., 2007; Javad et al., 2014; Maffei et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Diffusion-weighted MRI tractography has been used to identify the acoustic radiations between the auditory cortex and medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
source: Anatomical in vivo MRI investigations of the human subcortical auditory pathway so far have focused on thalamic nuclei (Devlin et al., 2006; Moerel et al., 2015), and the identification of the acoustic radiations between the auditory cortex and medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus with diffusion-weighted MRI tractography (Devlin et al., 2006; Behrens et al., 2007; Javad et al., 2014; Maffei et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The inferior colliculus of the midbrain can be identified using anatomical MRI.
source: The inferior colliculus of the midbrain can also be identified using anatomical MRI—for instance, Tourdias et al. (2014) and Moerel et al. (2015) show the inferior colliculus using short inversion time T1-weighted anatomical MRI at 7 Tesla, although neither investigation focused on anatomical segmentation of the inferior colliculus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Identification of the superior olivary complex and cochlear nucleus remain challenging with in vivo anatomical MRI due to their small size and deep locations.
source: Due to their small size and deep locations, identification of more caudal subcortical structures-the superior olivary complex and cochlear nucleus-remain challenging with in vivo anatomical MRI.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current MRI technology.

claim: Functional MRI (fMRI) has been used to investigate the relevance of subcortical processing of auditory information in humans.
source: Although lower spatial resolution than anatomical MRI, functional MRI (fMRI) has been used to investigate the relevance of subcortical processing of auditory information in humans, but it has been limited by the small size of the structures involved and the relatively low resolution attainable at conventional field strengths (3 Tesla and below) (Guimaraes et al., 1998; Harms and Melcher, 2002; Griffiths et al., 2001; Hawley et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous fMRI studies of subcortical auditory processing have been limited by the small size of the structures involved and the relatively low resolution attainable at conventional field strengths (3 Tesla and below).
source: Although lower spatial resolution than anatomical MRI, functional MRI (fMRI) has been used to investigate the relevance of subcortical processing of auditory information in humans, but it has been limited by the small size of the structures involved and the relatively low resolution attainable at conventional field strengths (3 Tesla and below) (Guimaraes et al., 1998; Harms and Melcher, 2002; Griffiths et al., 2001; Hawley et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous fMRI acquisitions required trade-offs, such as low through-plane resolution (7 mm) in exchange for moderate in-plane resolution (1.6 mm).
source: These acquisitions required trade-offs, such as low through-plane resolution (7 mm) in exchange for moderate in-plane resolution (1.6 mm), and in some cases researchers synchronized image collection to the cardiac cycle in order to overcame the physiological noise associated with blood pulsation in the brainstem (Guimaraes et al., 1998; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some researchers synchronized image collection to the cardiac cycle in order to overcome the physiological noise associated with blood pulsation in the brainstem.
source: These acquisitions required trade-offs, such as low through-plane resolution (7 mm) in exchange for moderate in-plane resolution (1.6 mm), and in some cases researchers synchronized image collection to the cardiac cycle in order to overcame the physiological noise associated with blood pulsation in the brainstem (Guimaraes et al., 1998; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) available at ultra-high magnetic fields (7 Tesla and above) has enabled higher resolution functional imaging of subcortical structures.
source: More recent advances in MRI, especially the increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) available at ultra-high magnetic fields (7 Tesla and above), have enabled higher resolution functional imaging of subcortical structures and more advanced localization of human auditory subcortical structures as well as their functional characterization.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of current MRI technology.

claim: De Martino et al. (2013) and Moerel et al. (2015) collected relatively high-resolution (1.1–1.5 mm isotropic) fMRI at 7 Tesla with an auditory paradigm to identify tonotopic gradients in the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus.
source: Using MRI at 7 Tesla (7T), De Martino et al. (2013) and Moerel et al. (2015) collected relatively high-resolution (1.1–1.5 mm isotropic) fMRI with an auditory paradigm to identify tonotopic gradients in the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A systematic comparison of the capabilities of different methodologies for imaging the subcortical auditory system has not yet been undertaken.
source: Despite the methodological advances in investigating the human brain, a systematic comparison of their capabilities for imaging the subcortical auditory system has not yet been undertaken.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The authors used publicly available histological data (Amunts et al., 2013) to segment the main nuclei along the subcortical auditory pathway.
source: Here, we use publicly available histological data (Amunts et al., 2013) to segment the main nuclei along the subcortical auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors evaluated the ability to identify subcortical auditory structures through postmortem anatomical MRI.
source: Using state-of-the-art acquisition and analysis techniques, we evaluate the ability to identify the same structures through postmortem anatomical MRI, through functional MRI using natural sounds, and through estimating the connectivity between subcortical auditory structures with postmortem and in vivo diffusion MRI tractography.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors evaluated the ability to identify subcortical auditory structures through functional MRI using natural sounds.
source: Using state-of-the-art acquisition and analysis techniques, we evaluate the ability to identify the same structures through postmortem anatomical MRI, through functional MRI using natural sounds, and through estimating the connectivity between subcortical auditory structures with postmortem and in vivo diffusion MRI tractography.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors evaluated the ability to estimate the connectivity between subcortical auditory structures with postmortem and in vivo diffusion MRI tractography.
source: Using state-of-the-art acquisition and analysis techniques, we evaluate the ability to identify the same structures through postmortem anatomical MRI, through functional MRI using natural sounds, and through estimating the connectivity between subcortical auditory structures with postmortem and in vivo diffusion MRI tractography.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors projected all images to MNI common reference space (Fonov et al., 2009; Fonov et al., 2011) to compare the histological, postmortem, and in vivo data.
source: To compare the histological, postmortem, and in vivo data, we project all images to MNI common reference space (Fonov et al., 2009; Fonov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors have made the postmortem anatomical data, in vivo functional and diffusion data, and the resulting atlases publicly available.
source: Finally, to facilitate dissemination of our results, we have made the postmortem anatomical data, in vivo functional and diffusion data, and the resulting atlases publicly available.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Post mortem MRI can provide similarly useful 3-D anatomical information as histology with less risk of tissue damage and warping.
source: Where histology provides ground truth information about neural anatomy, we show that post mortem MRI can provide similarly useful 3-D anatomical information with less risk of tissue damage and warping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In vivo functional MRI can reliably identify the subcortical auditory structures within individuals, even across experiments.
source: We also show that in vivo functional MRI can reliably identify the subcortical auditory structures within individuals, even across experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Each methodology (histology, postmortem MRI, in vivo MRI) successfully localized each of the small structures of the subcortical auditory system.
source: Overall, we found that each methodology successfully localized each of the small structures of the subcortical auditory system, and while known issues in image registration hindered direct comparisons between methodologies, each method provides complementary information about the human auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Known issues in image registration hindered direct comparisons between methodologies.
source: Overall, we found that each methodology successfully localized each of the small structures of the subcortical auditory system, and while known issues in image registration hindered direct comparisons between methodologies, each method provides complementary information about the human auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Each method (histology, postmortem MRI, in vivo MRI) provides complementary information about the human auditory pathway.
source: Overall, we found that each methodology successfully localized each of the small structures of the subcortical auditory system, and while known issues in image registration hindered direct comparisons between methodologies, each method provides complementary information about the human auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The authors manually segmented publicly available histological data (100 µm version of the BigBrain 3-D Volume Data Release 2015 in MNI space from https://bigbrain.loris.ca; Amunts et al., 2013).
source: To obtain a spatially accurate reference for all the subcortical auditory structures, we manually segmented publicly available histological data (100 µm version of the BigBrain 3-D Volume Data Release 2015 in MNI space from https://bigbrain.loris.ca; Amunts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The area around the inferior colliculus in the BigBrain dataset was incorrectly transformed into MNI space.
source: Upon inspecting this dataset, we noticed that the area around the inferior colliculus was incorrectly transformed into MNI space.
evidence: This is an observation made by the authors during data inspection.

claim: The incorrect transformation was causing the colliculi to be larger and more caudal than in the MNI reference brain.
source: This was causing the colliculi to be larger and more caudal than in the MNI reference brain (Figure 7, second and third panels).
evidence: This is an observation made by the authors, supported by Figure 7.

claim: The authors corrected the registration of the area around the colliculi.
source: Thus, our first step was to correctly register the area around the colliculi (Figure 7, fourth panel; see Materials and methods for details on the correction procedure).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study, supported by Figure 7.

claim: The authors acquired 50 µm isotropic voxel size 3-D gradient echo (GRE) MRI on a human postmortem brainstem and thalamus.
source: To delineate the subcortical auditory structures with MR histology, we acquired 50 µm isotropic voxel size 3-D gradient echo (GRE) MRI on a human postmortem brainstem and thalamus (described previously in Calabrese et al., 2015; see Materials and methods for additional details).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: Connectivity closely resembles the expected pattern of the human subcortical auditory wiring in the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography.
source: Connectivity closely resembles the expected pattern of the human subcortical auditory wiring.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Streamlines predominantly pass through the lateral lemniscus, the primary subcortical auditory tract.
source: In particular, streamlines predominantly pass through the lateral lemniscus, the primary subcortical auditory tract.
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Additional streamlines run through the brachium of the inferior colliculus, connecting the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate of the thalamus.
source: Additional streamlines run through the brachium of the inferior colliculus, connecting the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate of the thalamus.
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Many streamlines course rostrally toward the auditory cortex (not present in this specimen).
source: Many streamlines then course rostrally toward the auditory cortex (not present in this specimen).
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: At the caudal extent of the lateral lemniscus, streamlines pass through the superior olivary complex.
source: At the caudal extent of the lateral lemniscus, streamlines pass through the superior olivary complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Streamlines also run through the root of CNVIII.
source: Streamlines also run through the root of CNVIII.
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Each expected step along the subcortical auditory pathway is represented in the postmortem connectivity map.
source: In total, each expected step along the subcortical auditory pathway is represented in this connectivity map.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Connections tend to be between ipsilateral structures, with weak connectivity to contralateral structures other than commissural connections to the contralateral homolog (except for between the cochlear nuclei).
source: Overall, connections tend to be between ipsilateral structures, with weak connectivity to contralateral structures other than commissural connections to the contralateral homolog (except for between the cochlear nuclei).
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: The majority of streamlines pass through just one region (shown along the diagonal) in the postmortem connectivity analysis.
source: Still, the majority of streamlines pass through just one region (shown along the diagonal).
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: T2*-weighted GRE imaging is sensitive to blood vessels.
source: Because T2*-weighted GRE imaging is sensitive to blood vessels, we processed our anatomical MR image to highlight brainstem vasculature (Figure 5, right column, base image).
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of T2*-weighted GRE imaging.

claim: The 3-D vasculature images from postmortem MRI bear striking resemblance to post mortem data acquired with a stereoscopic microscope after full clearing method.
source: These 3-D vasculature images bear striking resemblance to post mortem data acquired with a stereoscopic microscope after full clearing method (see Duvernoy, 2013 for detailed diagrams of human brainstem vasculature).
evidence: This is a comparison made by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: The MGB and IC could be identified on the basis of the anatomical contrast in the participants.
source: Visual inspection and comparison to the MNI dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showed that the MGB and IC could be identified on the basis of the anatomical contrast in our participants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), especially in the short inversion time T1-weighted data (Tourdias et al., 2014; Moerel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo anatomical MRI data, supported by figures and citations.

claim: The superior olivary complex (SOC) could not be identified in average anatomical image from the 7T data.
source: However, while the superior olivary complex (SOC) could be identified in the MNI dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), it could not be identified in average anatomical image from our 7T data.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo anatomical MRI data, supported by figures.

claim: The inability to identify the SOC in the 7T data is possibly due to the limited number of subjects leading to the lower signal to noise in the average image.
source: This is possibly due to the limited number of subjects leading to the lower signal to noise in the average image.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for the inability to identify the SOC.

claim: Functional responses to 168 natural sounds (Experiment 1) were collected at 7T using a sparse acquisition scheme and a fast event-related design.
source: Functional responses to 168 natural sounds (Experiment 1) were collected at 7T using a sparse acquisition scheme and a fast event-related design.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The authors report the reproducibility of the individual functional delineations in six out of the 10 participants who participated in a follow up experiment (Experiment 2).
source: We additionally report the reproducibility of the individual functional delineations in six out of the 10 participants who participated in a follow up experiment in which responses to 96 natural sounds (Experiment 2) were collected at 7T using a sparse acquisition scheme and a fast event-related design.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: In all participants, clusters of significant activation in response to sounds were identified in the MGB, IC, SOC, and CN.
source: In all our participants, we could identify clusters of significant activation in response to sounds in the MGB, IC, SOC, and CN.
evidence: This is a finding from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: In each individual and for each auditory nucleus, activation clusters correspond to locations that are significantly active in at least three out of the other nine participants to the experiment.
source: In each individual and for each auditory nucleus, these activation clusters correspond to locations that are significantly active in at least three out of the other nine participants to the experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: The higher signal-to-noise ratio attainable in regions corresponding to the IC and MGB results in highly reproducible functional responses both within and across participants in these regions.
source: The higher signal-to-noise ratio attainable in regions corresponding to the IC and MGB results in highly reproducible functional responses both within and across participants in these regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: Activation clusters identified at the level of CN and SOC in single individuals also reproduce (albeit to a smaller degree with respect to IC and MGB), both within subjects (i.e. across experiments) and across subjects.
source: Activation clusters identified at the level of CN and SOC in single individuals also reproduce (albeit to a smaller degree with respect to IC and MGB), both within subjects (i.e. across experiments) and across subjects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: The clusters of voxels active in at least three out of the 10 participants at the level of the CN correspond mostly to the ventral part of CN.
source: At the level of the CN, the clusters of voxels active in at least three out of the 10 participants correspond mostly to the ventral part of CN.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: The dorsal subdivision of the CN is not recovered in the probabilistic maps (at least not in at least three volunteers consistently).
source: The dorsal subdivision of the CN is not recovered in these probabilistic maps (at least not in at least three volunteers consistently) possibly due to partial voluming with the nearby cerebrospinal fluid in combination with thinness (thickness around 0.5 mm) of the dorsal CN as it wraps around inferior cerebellar peduncle (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the functional MRI analysis, with speculation about the reason.

claim: The location of the activation clusters identifying the SOC overlaps with the SOC as identified in the BigBrain data.
source: Nearby, the location of the activation clusters identifying the SOC overlaps with the SOC as identified in the BigBrain data.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of functional MRI and histological data.

claim: The vasculature at the level of the SOC appears to have a specific orientation, with vessels draining blood from the center in a ventral direction.
source: In all subcortical regions, the vasculature appears to have a specific orientation, and, at the level of the SOC, vessels drain blood from the center in a ventral direction (i.e. the direction of draining is toward the surface of the brainstem in the top of the image reported in the transverse view, bottom in Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem MRI vasculature images.

claim: The specific vasculature architecture at the level of the SOC may result in the displacement or enlargement of the functionally defined clusters toward the ventral surface of the brainstem.
source: This specific vasculature architecture may result in the displacement or enlargement of the functionally defined clusters toward the ventral surface of the brainstem (as highlighted in the correspondence with histological data in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of vasculature on functional MRI results.

claim: The probability of the same voxel to be significantly modulated by sound presentation across subjects increased at the level of the IC and MGB.
source: The probability of the same voxel to be significantly modulated by sound presentation across subjects increased at the level of the IC and MGB, where the histologically defined regions corresponded (for the large part) to all subjects exhibiting significant responses to sounds.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: At the threshold of three subjects in the probabilistic maps, the IC seems to extend toward the superior direction, bordering and sometimes including parts of superior colliculus.
source: At the threshold of three subjects in the probabilistic maps, the IC seems to extend toward the superior direction, bordering and sometimes including parts of superior colliculus.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: The general directions of the vasculature penetrating the IC and draining blood towards the dorsal surface of brainstem angled in a superior direction may impact the functional definition of the IC.
source: On the other hand, similarly to what may happen in the SOC, the general directions of the vasculature penetrating the IC and draining blood towards the dorsal surface of brainstem angled in a superior direction (Figure 5 right panel) may also impact the functional definition of the IC.
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of vasculature on functional MRI results.

claim: The functional responses in the MGB cover an area that is in agreement with histological data.
source: The functional responses in the MGB cover an area that is in agreement with histological data.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of functional MRI and histological data.

claim: Compared to the IC or SOC, there is no major direction of extension of functional responses in the MGB.
source: Interestingly, compared to the IC or SOC, there is no major direction of extension of functional responses as well as no clear direction (in comparison to SOC and IC) of vascular draining.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: There is no clear direction of vascular draining in the MGB compared to the SOC and IC.
source: Interestingly, compared to the IC or SOC, there is no major direction of extension of functional responses as well as no clear direction (in comparison to SOC and IC) of vascular draining.
evidence: This is an observation from the postmortem MRI vasculature images.

claim: The high spatial and angular resolution of the in vivo diffusion data allow for vastly improved estimation of white matter connections between deep, small structures.
source: The high spatial and angular resolution of these data allow for vastly improved estimation of white matter connections between these deep, small structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the in vivo diffusion MRI data.

claim: The connectivity network from in vivo diffusion MRI appears to be dominated by laterality, in that left hemisphere structures are generally more connected with other left hemisphere structures.
source: Overall, the connectivity network appears to be dominated by laterality, in that left hemisphere structures are generally more connected with other left hemisphere structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: The cochlear nuclei and superior olivary complexes are strongly connected bilaterally in the in vivo diffusion MRI tractography.
source: However, there are a few notable exceptions to this pattern: the cochlear nuclei and superior olivary complexes are strongly connected bilaterally, which fits with animal research suggesting one-half to two-thirds of ascending auditory connections cross the midline at these early stages.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo diffusion MRI tractography results, with reference to animal research.

claim: There are a small number of connections between left and right inferior colliculi, likely along the anatomical commissure of the inferior colliculus.
source: Additionally, there are a small number of connections between left and right inferior colliculi, likely along the anatomical commissure of the inferior colliculus.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo diffusion MRI tractography results.

claim: Functional localization of the subcortical auditory system is achievable within each participant.
source: The auditory pathway includes a number of subcortical structures and connections, but identifying these components in humans has been challenging with existing in vivo imaging methods. We showed that functional localization of the subcortical auditory system is achievable within each participant, and that localization is consistent across experimental sessions.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Functional localization of the subcortical auditory system is consistent across experimental sessions.
source: The auditory pathway includes a number of subcortical structures and connections, but identifying these components in humans has been challenging with existing in vivo imaging methods. We showed that functional localization of the subcortical auditory system is achievable within each participant, and that localization is consistent across experimental sessions.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The authors created 3-D atlases of the human auditory pathway based on gold standard histology, 50 µm isotropic resolution post mortem anatomical MRI, and in vivo functional MRI at 7T.
source: To further facilitate research on the anatomy and function of the human subcortical auditory system, we created 3-D atlases of the human auditory pathway based on gold standard histology, 50 µm isotropic resolution post mortem anatomical MRI, and in vivo functional MRI at 7T.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: The authors created 3-D connectivity maps of the human subcortical auditory pathway using diffusion MRI tractography in a postmortem MRI sample and in living participants.
source: In addition, we created 3-D connectivity maps of the human subcortical auditory pathway using diffusion MRI tractography in a postmortem MRI sample and in living participants.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: The atlases and connectivity maps are the first fully 3-D representations of the human subcortical auditory pathway.
source: These atlases and connectivity maps are the first fully 3-D representations of the human subcortical auditory pathway and are publicly available to make the localization of subcortical auditory nuclei easier.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's contributions.

claim: The atlases are available in a common reference space (MNI152) to make registration to other MRI data as straightforward as possible.
source: In particular, the atlases are available in a common reference space (MNI152) to make registration to other MRI data as straightforward as possible.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the study's contributions.

claim: The authors improved the registration of the brainstem of BigBrain histological data to the MNI space.

claim: The use of slice acceleration allowed the authors to acquire enough slices to cover the whole brainstem, thalamus and cortical regions around Heschl's gyrus with the exclusion of anterior portions of the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
source: The use of slice acceleration (Moeller et al., 2010; Setsompop et al., 2012) allowed us to acquire enough slices to cover the whole brainstem, thalamus and cortical regions around Heschl's gyrus with the exclusion of anterior portions of the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the study, with reference to previous literature.

claim: Using isotropic voxels allowed the authors to better evaluate the 3-D volume of significantly activated regions, limiting partial volume effects that are inevitable when using thick anisotropic slices.
source: Using isotropic voxels allowed us to better evaluate the 3-D volume of significantly activated regions, limiting partial volume effects that are inevitable when using thick anisotropic slices.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the methods used in the study.

claim: Similar to previous research at lower magnetic fields, the 7T MR images did not allow for an anatomical definition of the CN and SOC (although IC and MGB were clearly visible).
source: Similar to previous research at lower magnetic fields (Hawley et al., 2005; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006), the 7T MR images did not allow for an anatomical definition of the CN and SOC (although IC and MGB were clearly visible).
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo anatomical MRI data, with reference to previous literature.

claim: A possible reason for the inability to anatomically define the CN and SOC is the reduced signal- and contrast-to-noise ratio in these regions.
source: A possible reason for this is the reduced signal- and contrast-to-noise ratio in these regions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for the inability to anatomically define the CN and SOC.

claim: Only very recently has 7T MRI enabled anatomical localization at the level of the SOC in individual subjects.
source: Only very recently has 7T MRI enabled anatomical localization at the level of the SOC in individual subjects (García-Gomar et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: The data show that functional mapping of the subcortical auditory pathway is an effective method for localizing these structures.
source: In contrast to in vivo anatomical localization, our data—in agreement with previous reports (Hawley et al., 2005; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006)—show that functional mapping of the subcortical auditory pathway is an effective method for localizing these structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional MRI analysis, with reference to previous literature.

claim: While histologically defined CN and SOC regions have been previously used to sample functional responses from in vivo fMRI data, the overlap between functionally and histologically defined subcortical auditory structures has not been reported before.
source: While histologically defined CN and SOC regions have been previously used to sample functional responses from in vivo fMRI data (Hawley et al., 2005; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006), the overlap between functionally and histologically defined subcortical auditory structures has not been reported before.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study, with reference to previous literature.

claim: Functional definitions of subcortical auditory structures are possible, as distinct clusters of activation were detected in all subjects across the subcortical auditory pathway.
source: We show that functional definitions are possible, as distinct clusters of activation were detected in all subjects across the subcortical auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional MRI analysis.

claim: These regions were reproducible both within subjects (across experiments) and across subjects (comparing single participants functional maps to the leave-one-out atlas obtained with all other participants).
